extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, logicians, mathematicians and theoretical physicists interested in foundations and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Identification and evaluation of strategies mathematicians use to assimilate or reinterpret 'anomalous' (non‑rigorous or paradoxical) techniques and objects originating in physics and engineering, and criteria for when such techniques count as mathematically meaningful. Includes attitudes, interpretive moves, and evidence used to justify assimilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of higher‑type objects for assimilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher types are useful in the process of assimilation because there are many more objects in higher types than in lower types; lower types can always be embedded in higher types but not conversely. Quantum mechanics uses variables of higher types: 'Instead of idealized points ... the primitive notion is a probability measure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides one to represent problematic lower‑level notions (point particles, functions) by richer higher‑type objects (measures, distributions), thereby explaining or justifying calculational practices from physics by moving to a higher‑type framework. Example: representing a quantum particle by a probability distribution rather than a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility theorems do not necessarily block mathematical sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Impossibility theorems often 'simply rule out certain obvious ways of interpreting' problematic techniques but do not preclude making mathematical sense of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with impossibility results (e.g., no classical 'Feynman measure'), seek alternative logics, reinterpretations, or reconstructions rather than dismissing the technique outright. The appropriate response can be a change in logic or a different formal framework that captures the successful computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy A — Prove physicists' results by conventional means
Attitude: dismiss anomalous objects as nonsense
rubrics_metrics.description: One possible attitude is to dismiss unruly objects (like the Dirac delta as originally presented) as nonsense because they violate classical mathematical definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logically impeccable but unhelpful in accounting for the empirical or calculational success of such devices; risks ignoring fruitful lines of practice in physics and engineering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude: accept contradictions pragmatically ('as long as it works')
rubrics_metrics.description: An extreme attitude (close to the physicists') is: 'Well, there's a contradiction, so what? As long as it works, that is all that matters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pragmatic stance allows continued use of unrigorous methods based on empirical success but may be philosophically and mathematically unsatisfactory. Paraconsistent logic is noted as related but of limited fruitfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical/critical attitude: reinterpret anomalous objects
rubrics_metrics.description: A nuanced approach is to 'maintain the view that the physicists’ calculations are largely correct, but that the objects they think they are talking about are in fact of a different nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to constructing new conceptual schemes (e.g., distributions, nonstandard analysis, modern umbral calculus) that make the physicists' computations rigorous by re‑casting the problematic objects in a different formal role (e.g., as linear operators). Illustrative example: Laurent Schwartz's theory of distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Push down higher‑order objects / adjoin ideal elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A common pattern is 'pushing down higher order objects' — taking higher order/type objects and promoting them to new objects at the bottom level; related is the historical method of 'adjoining ideal elements' to simplify and unify theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these moves to give a rigorous interpretation to dubious calculations. Examples: distributions for the Dirac delta, adjoining infinitesimals for certain interpretations, introduction of complex numbers or points at infinity in algebra/geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atiyah's strategy 1 — Prove heuristic results by other (rigorous) methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Atiyah's first strategy: mathematicians should 'take the heuristic results
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strategy emphasizes ignoring the physics background and focusing on establishing the mathematical results by conventional mathematical proof. It is reasonable but may fail to explain why the heuristics worked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atiyah's strategy 2 — Understand the physics and enter dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Atiyah's second approach: 'try to understand the physics involved and enter into a dialogue with physicists concerned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engaging with physicists can reveal the 'stage machinery' behind heuristics and can lead to deeper insight, but it may generate unease about standards (e.g., Jaffe and Quinn's concerns). Encourages interdisciplinary communication as a route to assimilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atiyah's strategy 3 — Develop the physics on a rigorous basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Atiyah's third approach: 'to try to develop the physics on a rigorous basis so as to give a formal justification to the conclusions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corresponds to building a rigorous mathematical formulation of the physical theory. Drawback: it can be too slow to keep up with active physics research; the gap between provable mathematics and current physical interest can be immense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atiyah's strategy 4 — Seek deeper meanings in physics‑mathematics connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Atiyah's fourth approach: 'to try to understand the deeper meanings of the physics‑mathematics connection' rather than treat mathematics merely as a tool for physics or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A visionary stance aiming at conceptual synthesis and uncovering fundamental connections; encourages long‑term conceptual research rather than immediate formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence criteria for accepting nonrigorous methods (applied to replica method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that a nonrigorous method has underlying mathematical sense includes: agreement with numerical simulations, predictions subsequently borne out by rigorous proofs, and broad applicability across different domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these empirical and mathematical signs as heuristics to judge when to invest effort in making a method rigorous. Example: the replica method produced predictions that matched simulations and were later verified in many cases (e.g., Talagrand's work proving Parisi's formula).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological warning about mathematical instability
rubrics_metrics.description: When physicists compute quantities using powerful but unrigorous methods and 'prove' them to their own satisfaction, the situation is 'mathematically unstable' because it eludes full mathematical formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematicians should either supply rigorous foundations or reinterpret the methods to explain why they work; otherwise the community risks relying on techniques whose justification is unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinterpretation tactics for specific anomalous objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete tactics: interpret the Dirac delta as a distribution (a linear operator on a class of functions), or reinterpret it via infinitesimals (a function with unit integral concentrated in an infinitesimal neighborhood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete reinterpretations make previously paradoxical manipulations rigorous within established or new formalisms (distribution theory, nonstandard analysis). The chosen tactic should match the restricted computational contexts in which the object appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plea for admitting nonrigorous mathematics into philosophical study
rubrics_metrics.description: Urges philosophers and logicians 'to look beyond the conventional boundaries of standard mathematics for mathematical work that is interesting but nonrigorous, with a view to making it rigorous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not relax standards of rigor, but expand the philosophical and logical study to include historical and contemporary nonrigorous practice as sources of fruitful mathematical development. Avoid defining mathematics so narrowly that pre‑1900 and other productive practices are excluded.
